title: The Hubble Space Telescope Is Sinking. NASA Is Looking for Ways to Keep It Afloat
gist: NASA has issued a Request for Information asking private companies to propose in-space servicing for the Hubble Space Telescope, which lacks propulsion and is expected to reenter in 2033 or 2034 unless boosted by about 2032; options include an orbit raise, upgrades, or controlled disposal, against a backdrop of a failed commercial reboost attempt for the Swift Observatory and Hubble's degraded gyros.

insights.claim: Because of atmospheric drag and the lack of an onboard propulsion system, NASA's analysis shows the Hubble Space Telescope will likely reenter Earth's atmosphere in 2033 or 2034 if left unchecked.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Sets a hard timeline for any commercial servicing contract opportunity.

insights.claim: NASA estimates a mission to raise Hubble's orbit would need to be carried out by 2032, and a higher, more stable orbit could let the telescope keep observing for several more years.

insights.claim: Hubble's hardware is also degrading: in June 2024 NASA switched it to a one-gyro operating mode after only three of six gyros remained operational and one began returning abnormal readings.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Hardware aging limits the value of a reboost and may shape upgrade proposals.

insights.claim: NASA has issued a formal Request for Information seeking private-sector proposals for in-space servicing of Hubble, including raising its altitude, upgrading its functionality, or managing a safe controlled reentry or disposal.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Opens a potential government demand signal for the nascent in-space servicing industry.

insights.claim: In September 2022, NASA signed a nonfunding partnership with SpaceX to study using the Dragon spacecraft to move Hubble to a more stable orbit, but the study only assessed commercial feasibility without plans for NASA to fund the mission.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: SpaceX has a head start as a potential Hubble reboost provider.

insights.claim: A NASA-commissioned orbital raise of the Swift Observatory by Katalyst Space Technologies failed when the company's spacecraft, launched in July 2026, suffered an attitude control malfunction, and Swift reentered the atmosphere over Indonesia on November 4.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Recent failure highlights execution risk for commercial in-space servicing firms and may raise NASA's bar for Hubble.

insights.claim: NASA administrator Jared Isaacman frames extending Hubble's life via innovative, cost-effective methods as an obligation to taxpayers and the scientific community.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Cost-effectiveness emphasis favors commercial bids over expensive government-run missions.
insights.quote: If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already in orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them.

insights.claim: Hubble was designed for astronaut servicing and has had five service missions since its 1990 launch, with the last—initially canceled after the 2003 Columbia disaster—carried out in 2009 to extend its lifespan.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Precedent shows NASA will reverse risk decisions when the scientific payoff is high.
